name: New Zealand
summary: New Zealand has no general capital gains tax, no inheritance, estate or gift tax and no net wealth tax, but a resident holding more than NZD 50,000 (cost) of foreign shares is taxed under the foreign investment fund (FIF) rules: normally 5% of the opening market value is deemed income (fair dividend rate), taxed at up to 39%, i.e. about 1.95% of the portfolio's value a year whatever the actual return (individuals may use the actual total return instead when it is lower, never below zero). Dividends and gains on those shares are not taxed separately. New residents get a once-only 4-year transitional-resident exemption on most foreign investment income, and since 2025 some new migrants can elect a realisation-based revenue account method (dividends plus 70% of gains), which US citizens can apply to all their foreign shares. Gains on residential property sold within 2 years (bright-line test) or on assets bought for resale are taxed.

regimes.name: New Zealand tax resident
regimes.description: Worldwide income taxed at up to 39% (above NZD 180,000); foreign portfolio shares taxed under the FIF rules.
regimes.eligibility: Resident with a permanent place of abode in New Zealand or after more than 183 days in any 12-month period.

capital_gains.summary: No comprehensive capital gains tax. Gains are taxed only where property was acquired for the purpose of disposal, in a profit-making scheme, by dealers, or on residential land sold within the 2-year bright-line period (main home excluded). Gains on foreign shares are not taxed on sale for a resident above the FIF threshold because the FIF regime taxes a deemed 5% return each year instead (recorded under wealth_tax).
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Bright-line test: residential land disposed of within 2 years of acquisition (disposals on or after 1 July 2024; previously up to 10 years). Main home exclusion.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Income Tax Act 2007 s CB 3/CB 4: gains on personal property (including shares) acquired with a dominant purpose of disposal are taxable at marginal rates. Financial arrangements (bonds, foreign-currency deposits) are taxed on accrual including FX gains. FIF holders leaving New Zealand are deemed to dispose of FIF interests at market value for FIF purposes.

capital_gains.rate_basis: No CGT for a long-term investor without a purpose of resale; local real estate outside the 2-year bright-line period. Foreign listed shares: 0% on sale because the FIF FDR method (modelled as a 1.95% annual levy in wealth_tax) replaces taxation of gains and dividends.
capital_gains.professional_trader: Share or property dealers, and anyone who acquired an asset for the dominant purpose of resale, are taxed on gains at marginal rates up to 39%. Purpose is a factual test; frequent trading is a risk.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: 2-year bright-line for residential land; no holding rule for shares.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Foreign shares above NZD 50,000 total cost: FIF regime (see wealth_tax). ASX-listed Australian resident companies that keep a franking account are exempt from FIF; their dividends are taxed, gains are not.

dividends.summary: New Zealand dividends carry imputation credits (company rate 28%); a top-rate shareholder pays 39% on the grossed-up dividend less the credit, about 15.3% of a fully imputed cash dividend. Foreign dividends on FIF interests valued under the FDR method are not taxed separately (the 5% deemed return replaces them). Below the NZD 50,000 de minimis, foreign dividends are taxed at up to 39% with a foreign tax credit.
dividends.exemptions_thresholds: FIF de minimis: total cost of attributing foreign interests NZD 50,000 or less.
dividends.important_exceptions: Australian franking credits are not usable in New Zealand. Foreign tax credits are limited to the treaty rate (e.g. 15%).

dividends.rate_basis: Domestic: fully imputed dividend D, taxable D/0.72, tax 39% x D/0.72 = 0.542D less credit 0.389D = 0.153D. Foreign: 0 because under FDR the dividends are subsumed in the 5% deemed return taxed under wealth_tax (1.95% of value); source WHT is credited against the FIF tax. A small portfolio (under NZD 50,000 cost) would pay 39% on foreign dividends instead.
dividends.withholding_outbound: NRWT on dividends: 0% on fully imputed dividends to 10%+ holders, 15% on fully imputed cash dividends to portfolio holders, 30% otherwise (treaty-reduced).
dividends.treaty_network: About 41 treaties (PwC table), including the US (15% portfolio dividends), Australia, UK and major EU states.
dividends.holding_company_notes: Company tax 28% with imputation. A New Zealand company holding the foreign portfolio pays FIF tax at 28% instead of 39% and is modelled as the 'investment_company' structure regime. Portfolio investment entities (PIEs) cap investor tax at 28% with no further tax on distributions, but a family cannot normally set up its own PIE (investor-number and other eligibility rules), so this applies to investing through public PIE funds rather than to a family vehicle.

wealth_tax.summary: No net wealth tax. However, the FIF fair dividend rate method taxes 5% of the opening market value of foreign shares each year as income (39% top rate = about 1.95% of value), regardless of actual dividends or gains. It is recorded here as a limited levy on foreign financial assets because economically it works like one.
wealth_tax.exemptions_thresholds: Applies only if the total cost of foreign attributing interests exceeds NZD 50,000 at any time in the year. Exempt: ASX-listed Australian-resident companies with franking accounts. Individuals and eligible family trusts may instead pay on the actual total return (comparative value) when it is lower than 5%, and the portfolio total cannot go below zero.
wealth_tax.important_exceptions: Statutory basis: Income Tax Act 2007 subpart EX (FIF rules), FDR method. Budget 2026 proposals (IRD information sheet, 28 May 2026; not yet law, bill status not confirmed): all residents could use the revenue account method for unlisted foreign shares only, residents taxed twice because of citizenship or a right to work elsewhere (mainly US citizens) could use the extended RAM for all foreign shares, and the FIF de minimis would rise from NZD 50,000 to NZD 100,000 from 1 April 2026 if enacted. A listed portfolio held by an EU family stays under the FDR method.

components.name: FIF fair dividend rate (5% deemed return taxed at 39%)
components.notes: Threshold is on total cost, not value, and is not indexed (set in 2000; IRD's Budget 2026 information sheet proposes raising it from NZD 50,000 to NZD 100,000). Rate = 5% x 39% top marginal rate. Foreign source dividend WHT is creditable against it. In loss or low-return years individuals can pay on the actual return (comparative value), floor zero.

wealth_tax.property_tax_note: Local council rates on land based on rateable value. No stamp duty on property. Residential land withholding tax applies to offshore sellers within the bright-line period.

inheritance.summary: No inheritance, estate or gift tax. Estate duty was abolished in 1992 and gift duty for transfers made on or after 1 October 2011 (Inland Revenue's gift duty abolition note and gifting overview, found by search and not opened). Transfers to children are tax-free; for FIF shares the heirs simply continue under the FIF rules.
inheritance.important_exceptions: Inherited residential land is generally outside the bright-line test for the heir (general rule; not verified). Trusts: trustee income tax rate 39% from 2024/25 (not verified in this session).

regimes.name: Transitional resident (4-year exemption)
regimes.description: New migrants and New Zealanders returning after 10 years are exempt for about 4 years on most foreign income: foreign interest, dividends, FIF income, rent and gains. Foreign employment and personal-services income is not exempt.
regimes.eligibility: Became tax resident on or after 1 April 2006, not tax resident at any time in the previous 10 years, never transitional before. Ends 4 years after the end of the month of qualifying, or earlier on opting out (e.g. claiming Working for Families credits). Automatic; opting out is irrevocable.

capital_gains.summary: Foreign-source gains (e.g. on foreign shares) are exempt during the transitional period; New Zealand-source gains taxed as for residents (generally none).

sources.title: Transitional tax residents exemption

capital_gains.rate_basis: Foreign-source income and FIF income exempt during the 4-year period; domestic gains as standard.

dividends.summary: Foreign dividends need not be declared and the FIF rules do not apply during the transitional period. NZ dividends taxed as standard.

regimes.name: Revenue account method for new migrants (extended RAM for foreign citizens taxed abroad, e.g. US citizens)
regimes.description: Introduced on 30 March 2026 (IRD, Budget 2026 information sheet), eligible new residents who became resident on or after 1 April 2024 after at least five years of non-residence may elect to tax qualifying FIF shares on a realisation basis: dividends at marginal rates plus 70% of realised gains. Under 'extended RAM' it applies to all foreign shares of a person who remains liable to tax on their disposal in another country by citizenship or right to live there (in practice US citizens). Leaving New Zealand triggers a deferred deemed disposal for 3 years.
regimes.eligibility: Natural person (or family trust whose principal settlor qualifies) who became resident (not transitional) on or after 1 April 2024 after at least five years of non-residence. Without the extended rule RAM covers only unlisted foreign shares acquired before arrival, so for a listed portfolio it is relevant mainly to US citizens.

capital_gains.summary: Gains on RAM foreign shares are taxed on sale at 70% x marginal rate = 27.3% at the 39% rate; losses only offset RAM gains/dividends.

capital_gains.rate_basis: 0.7 x realised gain x 39% = 27.3% on foreign shares under RAM; other assets as standard.

dividends.summary: Dividends on RAM shares are taxed when received at marginal rates (39% top) with a foreign tax credit.

regimes.duration_note: RAM is an election, not a time-limited concession: once a qualifying migrant elects it, it keeps applying to the elected FIF interests while the person remains resident; it ends only on leaving New Zealand (deemed disposal, deferred for 3 years).

regimes.name: New Zealand investment holding company (28% company tax on FIF income)
regimes.description: The family's foreign portfolio is held by a New Zealand company. Under the foreign investment fund (FIF) rules the company is taxed on a deemed 5% return (fair dividend rate) at the 28% company rate, 1.4% of value a year, instead of 1.95% at the 39% personal rate. Actual dividends and gains on the foreign shares are not taxed separately; New Zealand has no general capital gains tax. Distributions to the family carry imputation credits for the 28% already paid, leaving 11 points to pay at the 39% rate.
regimes.eligibility: Any New Zealand-resident family once the 4-year transitional-resident exemption is over (during it, holding personally is better: foreign investment income is exempt for the individual but not for a New Zealand company). Not useful for US persons (the company is a PFIC/CFC for US tax) or for migrants using the revenue account method, which only natural persons and family trusts can elect.
regimes.duration_note: Ordinary company taxation with no time limit; it lasts as long as the company holds the portfolio and the family stays resident.

structure.entity: New Zealand limited company (investment holding company)
structure.payout_notes: Dividends are taxable to resident shareholders with imputation credits for company tax paid: at the 39% rate, a fully imputed dividend D costs 39% x D/0.72 - 0.389D = 15.3% of the cash. The company's FIF income (5% of a foreign portfolio of roughly NZD 50 million, about NZD 2.5 million a year) generates enough imputation credits to fully impute the family's withdrawals. Cash paid out of untaxed surpluses (actual returns above the deemed 5%) carries no credits and is taxed at 39%, except that realised capital gains can be paid out tax-free on liquidation (s CD 26 / CD 44, BR Pub 14/09). Resident withholding tax applies to dividends at 33% less imputation credits; shareholder loans need market interest.
structure.substance_and_anti_avoidance: Running cost is a reasoned estimate, not sourced (annual financial statements, company income tax return with FIF and imputation calculations, Companies Office annual return). A company must use the fair dividend rate (or other prescribed) method: it cannot switch to the comparative value method in years when the actual return is below 5%, has no NZD 50,000 de minimis, and cannot claim FIF losses, so in bad years it pays 1.4% while an individual could pay 0. ASX-listed Australian companies are outside the FIF rules; their dividends are taxed to the company with franking not creditable. Gains on shares held for resale are taxable income (dealer test). The general anti-avoidance rule (s BG 1, Penny and Hooper) targets arrangements that divert personal income into a company; holding a passive portfolio in a company is a long-accepted choice, but the 2024 increase of the trustee rate to 39% came with integrity rules on income routed through close companies (s HC 38, not verified). The trustee rate itself is 39%, so a family trust offers no rate advantage.
structure.exit_and_liquidation: New Zealand has no exit tax for individuals emigrating; the company stays resident while managed in New Zealand. On liquidation, subscribed capital and realised capital gains are returned tax-free, and the rest (including retained FIF income) is a dividend with imputation credits. Dividends paid to shareholders who have become non-resident bear non-resident withholding tax (rates not verified here).

capital_gains.summary: No capital gains tax for the company on long-term investments. Gains on foreign shares are covered by the FIF deemed 5% return (recorded under wealth_tax); gains on New Zealand and ASX-listed shares held on capital account are untaxed. Shares bought for resale are taxed at 28%.
capital_gains.rate_basis: As for an individual: no general CGT; FIF interests taxed through the fair dividend rate instead of on realisation. Real estate as standard (outside the 2-year bright-line test). The difference is that untaxed gains can only leave the company tax-free on liquidation.
capital_gains.professional_trader: A company that deals in shares, or bought them with a dominant purpose of resale, is taxed on gains at 28%.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Foreign shares under 10%: FIF rules (fair dividend rate) instead of tax on gains.

dividends.summary: Foreign portfolio dividends are not taxed separately: they are covered by the FIF deemed return (5% of value at 28%), with foreign withholding tax credited. New Zealand dividends received with full imputation credits bear no further tax in the company.
dividends.rate_basis: Domestic: fully imputed dividend D, taxable D/0.72, tax 28% x D/0.72 = 0.389D less credit 0.389D = 0. Foreign: 0 here because the FIF fair dividend rate (5% x 28% = 1.4% of value, under wealth_tax) replaces tax on the dividend; source WHT credited against the FIF tax. Dividends from ASX-listed Australian companies (outside FIF) are taxed at 28%.
dividends.holding_company_notes: Company tax 28% (PwC). A New Zealand company's foreign dividends are generally exempt income; portfolio interests are instead taxed under the FIF rules, and dividends from FIF-exempt portfolio holdings (e.g. ASX-listed Australian companies) are taxable (PwC).

us_citizen_notes: US citizens are taxed by the US on worldwide gains and dividends; the FIF deemed income can create a timing mismatch with US realisation-based taxation and foreign tax credit problems. The extended revenue account method (introduced 30 March 2026) lets eligible US citizens who arrived on or after 1 April 2024 after 5 years abroad tax all foreign shares on realisation (dividends + 70% of gains), which aligns better with US timing. The transitional resident exemption also applies.
open_questions: The FIF FDR charge is modelled as a 'limited' wealth-tax component (1.95% of foreign share value above NZD 50,000 cost) because the schema has no deemed-income field; foreign dividends and gains are set to 0 to avoid double counting.

Budget 2026 FIF proposals (RAM for unlisted shares for all residents, extended RAM for people taxed twice, de minimis NZD 100,000): IRD's information sheet of 28 May 2026 was read, but whether the bill is introduced or passed was not confirmed.
The gift duty (1 October 2011) and estate duty (1992) abolition dates come from search results of Inland Revenue pages, which were not opened.
